topic: raising copper vessels: annealing between courses, even walls, planishing and tinning the inside

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-6)
provenance.notes: pisane niezaleznie, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: czujnik zegarowy do pomiaru scianki na warsztacie

base: I have started raising copper pans from flat sheet and the rim keeps cracking as it comes up.
An old kettle hangs by the range and was tinned by my grandfather forty years ago.
A dial gauge lies on the bench so that I can check the wall as it thins.
I hammered the first pan down over a stake for an hour without once stopping to anneal it.
Is the cracking a fault in the sheet, or am I simply working the copper too hard?
You are working it too hard, since copper hardens under the hammer and will split before long.
Anneal after every course of hammering, which in raising means every ten minutes or so.
Heat it to a dull red in a dim corner of the shop and quench it at once.
Judged in bright daylight you will overheat the copper and lose the very edge you are raising.
I annealed after every course and the second pan came up without a crack anywhere in it.
The dial gauge shows the wall down to half its starting thickness near the rim.
That worries me, because the base is still as thick as the sheet I began with.
Should the wall thin like that, or have I moved the metal in the wrong direction?
Some thinning is unavoidable, but half is too much and tells you the blows fell too near the rim.
Raising should move metal inward from the edge, gathering it rather than stretching it out.
Work in courses that begin near the base and travel outward, not the other way about.
A pan thin at the rim and thick at the base will always ring dead when struck.
I worked the courses outward from the base and the third pan has kept an even wall.
It rings properly now, much as the old kettle does when I tap it on the side.
The surface is covered in hammer marks and looks rough beside anything from a shop.
I understand that planishing smooths it, though I do not know what hammer to use.
Should the planishing hammer be flat across the face, or slightly domed like a ball?
Slightly domed, and polished until you can see your own face in the striking surface.
A flat face leaves edge marks that show up as fine crescents under any strong light.
Planish over a stake that matches the curve, so every blow lands on supported metal.
Work in overlapping rows and never come back over a row you have already finished.
The marks should read as a regular skin, since evenness matters far more than smoothness.
The planished skin came out even and the pan looks like a proper piece of work.
Now I want to tin the inside and have a bar of tin and some resin ready.
My first attempt left bare patches where the tin refused to take at all.
Was the copper not clean enough, or did I simply have the pan too cool?
Bare patches almost always mean grease, since tin will not wet copper that has been handled.
Scour it with sand and a cut lemon, then rinse and do not touch the surface again.
Bring the pan to the heat where a wiped rag leaves a bright, wet line behind it.
Too cool and the tin sits in beads, too hot and it burns and goes grey.
Scouring with sand and lemon did it and the tin ran right out to the rim.
The pan has been in daily use since spring and the tin is wearing thin at the centre.
The old kettle has been tinned only once in living memory and still looks perfectly sound.
Does a pan need retinning that often, or is mine wearing faster than it should?
A pan in daily use wears faster than a kettle, which only ever holds water.
Stirring with metal spoons takes off more tin in a month than heat does in a year.
Use wood in it and the coat will last you five years rather than one.
When it does go, have the whole inside stripped and tinned again rather than patched.
